label: Shaped Christian Neoplatonic cosmology and rational anthropology
description: Hildegard drew on Augustinian illumination and Trinitarian psychology while elevating material nature and bodily vitality as active reflections of divine wisdom.
dialecticalTension: Counters dualistic contempt for physical matter with sacramental affirmation of ecological vitality.

citations.author: Barbara Newman
citations.work: Sister of Wisdom: St. Hildegard's Theology of the Feminine

label: Transmitted cosmic harmony and the personification of Wisdom (Sapientia)
description: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy and cosmic music theory resonated deeply in Hildegard's Liber Divinorum Operum and Symphonia, uniting cosmic order, sound, and soul.
dialecticalTension: Connects late-antique cosmic harmony with medieval natural philosophy and medicine.
historicalContext: Medieval monastic curriculum centered on Boethian treatises.

label: Formulated the metaphysical concept of viriditas (cosmic greening vitality)
description: Hildegard conceived viriditas as the verdant, self-renewing power connecting botanical life, human bodily health, and moral-spiritual flourishing.
dialecticalTension: Bridges medieval metaphysics, ecology, and holistic natural philosophy.
historicalContext: Developed in Scivias (1151), Physica, and Liber Divinorum Operum (1174).

label: Prefigured vitalist monism of living, interconnected created nature
description: Hildegard's rejection of inert matter in favor of pervasive living vitality (viriditas) prefigured early modern vitalist philosophies such as Anne Conway's vitalist monadism.
dialecticalTension: Traces a cross-century lineage of vitalist non-mechanistic natural philosophy.
historicalContext: Historical continuity from 12th-century natural philosophy to 17th-century vitalism.
